disease_name: Acute kidney injury / 急性腎障害

distillation_scope.disease_name_input: Acute kidney injury / 急性腎障害
distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer clinical disease leaf for abrupt kidney excretory failure. Prerenal physiology, intrinsic tubular/glomerular/microvascular injury, postrenal obstruction, contrast exposure, rhabdomyolysis, sepsis, cardiorenal physiology, and nephrotoxin exposure are represented as mechanisms, context axes, risk factors, or future second-layer subtypes rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking should use abrupt creatinine/BUN rise, falling eGFR, oliguria/anuria, electrolyte and acid-base retention, fluid overload, uremic features, urinalysis pattern, obstruction imaging, nephrotoxin or contrast context, and RRT need when those facts are available. Etiologic labels and treatment response remain structured context, not hard diagnostic labels.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Low effective arterial volume, hypotension, renal venous congestion, heart failure, cirrhosis physiology, bleeding, dehydration, or vasodilation lowers glomerular filtration pressure and can be reversible if corrected early.

Ischemia, sepsis, pigment nephropathy, contrast, toxins, drugs, tumor lysis, and inflammatory stress injure tubular epithelium, causing impaired filtration, concentrating defects, granular casts, and delayed recovery.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: 糸球体・微小血管障害
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Immune-complex nephritis, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, infection-related glomerulonephritis, TMA, malignant hypertension, vasculitis, or endothelial injury produces active urinary sediment, proteinuria, hematuria, and abrupt GFR loss.

Bilateral ureteral obstruction, bladder outlet obstruction, solitary kidney obstruction, clots, stones, tumor, retroperitoneal disease, or catheter obstruction raises collecting-system pressure and acutely reduces GFR.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: 濾過低下・高窒素血症
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Abrupt GFR loss raises creatinine and BUN, lowers estimated GFR, and accumulates uremic solutes; BUN may be disproportionately high with catabolism, bleeding, steroids, or volume depletion.
Reduced urine output and sodium-water excretion cause edema, weight gain, pulmonary congestion, respiratory failure, and diuretic or renal replacement therapy context.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: 電解質・酸塩基保持障害
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Impaired renal excretion and tubular handling produce hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, phosphate retention, sodium disturbances, ECG instability, and dialysis indications.
Severe or prolonged AKI can cause encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding tendency, nausea, anorexia, immune dysfunction, dialysis dependence, and mortality hazard.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Lower filtration pressure can rapidly lower GFR and raise creatinine/BUN.
Sustained ischemia converts functional renal hypoperfusion into tubular injury.
Tubular injury reduces filtration, secretion, and creatinine/BUN clearance.
Glomerular inflammation or microvascular occlusion lowers filtration surface and renal blood flow.
Back pressure from urinary obstruction rapidly lowers net filtration pressure.
Creatinine rises as filtration falls.
BUN rises with reduced renal clearance and catabolic or volume-depleted contexts.
Estimated GFR falls as filtration failure worsens.
AKI stage integrates creatinine rise and urine-output criteria.
Oliguric AKI reduces daily urine volume.
Oliguria is clinically measured by mL/kg/hour urine output.
Low urine output is the parent finding for oliguria.
Reduced salt-water excretion promotes fluid overload.
Reduced renal potassium excretion raises serum potassium.
Reduced acid excretion and tubular dysfunction lower bicarbonate.
Acid retention produces a metabolic acidosis finding.
Uremic toxins can cause altered mental status when severe or prolonged.
Uremic symptoms, electrolyte derangements, acidosis, and fluid overload increase dialysis need.
Postrenal AKI requires a urinary obstruction context.
Obstruction commonly causes hydronephrosis when imaging is performed.
Muddy brown granular casts support intrinsic tubular injury.

axes.clinical_interpretation: Lifespan outcome hazard from AKI severity, hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, uremia, shock, and multiorgan context.
AST can rise substantially from skeletal muscle injury in rhabdomyolysis-associated AKI; this is a source-context muscle injury signal, not a liver-specific label.
ALT can rise moderately in severe rhabdomyolysis-associated AKI and should be interpreted with CK/myoglobin rather than as isolated hepatocellular disease.
LDH rises with muscle injury, hemolysis, ischemia, and multiorgan stress in severe AKI contexts.
Heme-positive urine without infection can reflect pigment load from rhabdomyolysis or hemolysis and supports pigment nephropathy context.
Marked fluid overload can emerge when severe oliguria/anuria prevents excretion and often contributes to dialysis indication.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Higher creatinine mathematically and clinically corresponds to lower eGFR.
Creatinine and BUN are both downstream of filtration failure, though BUN has additional context modifiers.
Low measured urine output defines oliguria.
Oliguria reduces salt-water clearance and raises volume overload probability.
Fluid overload can manifest as pulmonary edema.
Clinically significant overload increases respiratory and ICU risk.
The hyperkalemia finding is driven by the measured potassium value.
Severe or rapidly rising potassium increases malignant arrhythmia hazard.
Severe metabolic acidosis can destabilize cardiovascular and respiratory physiology.
Obstruction often produces hydronephrosis, especially when bilateral or prolonged.
Active urinary sediment often includes hematuria, but either can be incompletely reported.
Severe rhabdomyolysis can drive myoglobin-mediated tubular injury.
Dialysis-requiring AKI marks severe kidney failure and often multiorgan illness.
Hyperkalemic arrhythmia is an immediate mortality pathway.
Pulmonary edema and fluid overload can worsen oxygenation and survival.
Severe acidemia contributes to hemodynamic and respiratory collapse.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Volume repletion is most useful when low effective circulating volume is active.
Additional fluid can worsen pulmonary edema or congestion.

side_effects.interpretation: Fluid can worsen overload when renal excretion or cardiac reserve is limited.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Exposure removal is most relevant when a drug, toxin, or contrast burden is active.
Low eGFR increases drug accumulation and toxicity risk.
Decompression only addresses an obstructive driver.
Feasible catheter, stent, nephrostomy, or surgery makes obstruction relief more effective.
Diuretics are used to move fluid when overload is active.
Anuria implies little tubular response to diuretics.
Preserved urine response is needed for loop diuretic decongestion.

side_effects.interpretation: Overdiuresis can worsen effective volume and renal perfusion.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: RRT is useful when refractory electrolyte, acid-base, volume, uremic, or severe azotemic complications are active.
Access or anticoagulation barriers can delay effective RRT.
Shock or cardiac instability changes the tolerated dialysis mode.
Alkali support is meaningful when metabolic acidosis is present.
Sodium load can worsen volume overload.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Lower nephron reserve raises AKI susceptibility, creatinine baseline, dialysis need, and nonrecovery risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: CKD raises baseline and peak creatinine for the same acute hit.
Baseline eGFR is lower and can fall into dialysis-range values.
Low reserve raises persistent dysfunction risk.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Vascular disease, diabetes, frailty, and older age reduce renal autoregulatory reserve and increase tubular, glomerular, and recovery vulnerability.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Tubular injury risk is higher for the same hemodynamic or toxic exposure.
Age and frailty increase short-term AKI mortality.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, calcineurin inhibitors, amphotericin, cisplatin, IV contrast, toxins, or combinations can trigger or amplify AKI.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Exposure context anchors intrinsic tubular or hemodynamic injury.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Removing the ongoing exposure is more important when exposure is active.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding, diuretics, poor intake, sepsis vasodilation, cirrhosis, heart failure, or third spacing lowers effective renal perfusion.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: BUN can be disproportionately high in volume depletion.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Fluid resuscitation directly addresses low effective volume.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Bilateral obstruction, solitary kidney obstruction, urinary retention, catheter blockage, ureteral stones, tumor, or retroperitoneal disease can abruptly cause postrenal AKI.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Postrenal mechanism becomes the dominant driver.
Imaging obstruction evidence is more likely.

risk_factors.clinical_rationale: Severe muscle injury or pigment load can cause intrinsic tubular injury, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and dialysis-requiring AKI.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Cellular potassium release can amplify hyperkalemia.

supportive_care: Trend creatinine, BUN, eGFR, urine output, potassium, bicarbonate, pH, phosphate, volume status, and medication dosing at a cadence matched to AKI severity.
Use parent findings plus measurements: oliguria/anuria should include raw urine output when available; fluid overload should include pulmonary edema or weight gain when reported.
Review and stop or dose-adjust nephrotoxins; avoid repeat contrast exposure when safer diagnostic routes can answer the same question.
Evaluate reversible obstruction with bladder scan, catheter patency check, renal ultrasound, CT, or urology procedure when postrenal context is plausible.
Coordinate nephrology, critical care, and source-control teams when hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, pulmonary edema, uremic symptoms, or dialysis need is active.
Preserve etiologic context as axes or risk factors; do not collapse sepsis, rhabdomyolysis, obstruction, contrast exposure, or drug toxicity into disease-id qualifiers.
